'''''Onopordum acanthium''''' ('''cotton thistle''', '''[[Thistle#Scottish thistle|Scotch (or Scottish) thistle]])''' is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]]. It is native to Europe and [[Western Asia]] from the [[Iberian Peninsula]] east to [[Kazakhstan]], and north to central [[Scandinavia]], and widely [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] elsewhere,<ref name="Stace">{{cite book |author=Clive A. Stace |year=2010 |title=New Flora of the British Isles |url=https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac |url-access=limited |edition=3rd |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge |isbn=978-0-521-70772-5 |page=[https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac/page/n730 695]|author-link=Clive A. Stace}}</ref><ref>[http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/astera/onopo/onopaca.html Den virtuella floran: ''Onopordum acanthium'' (in Swedish, with maps)]</ref><ref name=Europaea>[http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Onopordum&SPECIES_XREF=acanthium&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK=Flora Europaea: ''Onopordum acanthium''] {{Dead link|date=January 2022}}</ref> with especially large populations present in the [[United States of America|United States]] and [[Australia]]. It is a vigorous [[biennial plant]] with coarse, spiny leaves and conspicuous spiny-winged stems.<ref name=Tutin>Tutin, T. G. et al., eds. (1976). ''Flora Europaea'' vol. 4. Cambridge University Press {{ISBN|0-521-08717-1}}</ref>

It should not be confused with ''[[Cirsium vulgare]]'' (spear thistle), which is also known as Scotch or Scottish thistle and is the [[Floral emblem|national flower]] of Scotland.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022|reason=I can find no reliable sources that the national flower of Scotland is defined beyond "thistle".}}  Spear thistle is native to Britain, while cotton thistle is non-native.

==Description==
[[File:Eselsdistel.JPG|thumb|left|upright|Detailed image]]
It is a biennial plant, producing a large [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of spiny [[Leaf|leaves]] the first year. The plants typically germinate in the autumn after the first rains and exist as rosettes throughout the first year, forming a stout, fleshy [[taproot]] that may extend down {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on}} or more for a food reserve.

In the second year, the plant can grow to as much as {{convert|3|m|abbr=on}} tall with a width of up to {{convert|1.5|m|abbr=on}}. The leaves are {{convert|10|-|50|cm|abbr=on}} wide, alternate, spiny, and often covered with white woolly hairs with the lower surface more densely covered than the upper. The leaves are deeply lobed with long, stiff spines along the margins. Fine hairs give the plant a greyish appearance. The massive main stem may be {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on}} wide at the base and branched in the upper part. Each stem has a vertical row of broad, spiny wings (conspicuous ribbon-like leafy material), typically {{convert|2|-|3|cm|abbr=on}} wide, extending to the base of the flower head.

The [[flower]]s are globe shaped, {{convert|2|-|6|cm|abbr=on}} in diameter, from dark pink to lavender, and are produced in the summer. The flower buds form first at the tip of the stem and later at the tip of the axillary branches. They appear singly or in groups of two or three on branch tips. The plants are androgynous, with both [[Gynoecium|pistil]] and [[stamen]]s, and sit above numerous, long, stiff, spine-tipped [[bract]]s, all pointing outwards, the lower ones wider apart and pointing downwards. After flowering, the [[Ovary (plants)|ovary]] starts swelling and forms about 8,400 to 40,000 seeds per plant.<ref name=Tutin/><ref>[http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3864 Flora of NW Europe: Cotton Thistle]{{Dead link|date=April 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref><ref>Young, J.A. and R.A. Evans. 1969. "Control and ecological studies of Scotch thistle". Weed Science 17:60-63.</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Cotton thistles are native to [[Eurasia]]. The plant prefers [[Habitat (ecology)|habitats]] with dry summers, such as the Mediterranean region, growing best in sandy clay and calcareous [[soil]]s which are rich in [[ammonium]] salts. It grows in [[Ruderal species|ruderal]] places, as well as in dry pastures and fields. Its preferred habitats are natural areas, disturbed sites, roadsides, fields, and especially sites with fertile soils, agricultural areas, range/grasslands, riparian zones, scrub/shrublands valleys and plains along with water courses.<ref name="Stace"/><ref name=Tutin/> Temperature and moisture, rather than soil nutrient concentrations, determine the ecological performance of ''Onopordum'' species.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=M. P. Austin |author2=R. H. Groves |author3=L. M. F. Fresco |author4=P. E. Kaye |year=1985 |title=Relative growth of six thistle species along a nutrient gradient with multispecies competition |journal=[[Journal of Ecology]] |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=667–684 |jstor=2260503|doi=10.2307/2260503}}</ref>

In Europe, the plant tends to colonise disturbed pastures. In its native range, cotton thistle is considered a weak competitor that needs regeneration gaps to develop and maintain stands; populations tend to retreat when disturbance ceases.<ref name="Mucina">{{cite journal |author=Ladislav Mucina |year=1989 |title=Syntaxonomy of the ''Onopordum acanthium'' communities in temperate and continental Europe |journal=[[Vegetatio]] |volume=81 |issue=1–2 |pages=107–115 |doi=10.1007/BF00045516 |jstor=20038441|s2cid=35269104 |author-link=Ladislav Mucina}}</ref> The plant has been widely introduced at mid-latitudes across much of North America.<ref>Taylor, R. J. 1990. "Northwest Weeds: The Ugly and Beautiful Villains of Fields, Gardens, and Roadsides". Mountain Press Publishing, Missoula, Montana.</ref>

Scotch thistles can spread rapidly. For example, it was first found in Utah in 1963. By 1981, it covered approximately 6070 hectares in 17 counties. Eight years later, it had spread to cover more than 22,540 hectares in 22 counties.<ref>Dewey, S.A. (1991). Weed thistles of the western United States. In: James, L. F., J. O. Evans, M. H. Ralphs, and R. D. Child, eds. ''Noxious Range Weeds''. Westview Press, Boulder, Colorado, pp. 247-253.</ref>

==Ecology==
''Onopordum acanthium'' reproduces by seeds only. Most seeds [[germinate]] in autumn after the first rains, but some seeds can germinate year round under favourable moisture and temperature conditions. Seeds that germinate in late autumn become biennials. When they germinate earlier, they can behave as annuals. Buried seed can remain viable in the [[soil seed bank]] for at least seven years, possibly for up to twenty years or more. Yearly seed production and [[seed dormancy]] are highly variable, depending on environmental conditions.

The slender and smooth [[achenes]] are about 3 mm long, brown with gray markings. They are tipped with a pappus of slender bristles. Mainly locally dispersed by wind, or more widely by humans, birds, wildlife, livestock or streams, the seeds are sensitive to light and only germinate when close to the surface. Seedlings will emerge from soil depths up to 4.5 cm, 0.5 cm are optimal.<ref name=Tutin/> While some seeds will germinate in the dark, most germination occurs with alternating light/dark cycles, with an optimal day length of eight hours.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=James A. Young|author2=Raymond A. Evans|name-list-style=amp |year=1972 |title=Germination and persistence of achenes of Scotch thistle |journal=[[Weed Science]] |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=98–101 |jstor=4042041|doi=10.1017/S0043174500035049|s2cid=83133668 }}</ref>

The leaves of cotton thistle are eaten by the [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]], such as the [[thistle ermine]] (''Myelois circumvoluta'').

==Taxonomy and naming==
Three subspecies are accepted:<ref name=Tutin/>
*''Onopordum acanthium'' subsp. ''acanthium''. Most of the species' range.
*''Onopordum acanthium'' subsp. ''gautieri'' (Rouy) Franco. France, Spain.
*''Onopordum acanthium'' subsp. ''parnassicum'' (Boiss. & Heldr.) Nyman. Greece.

The genus botanical name is derived from the [[Ancient Greek]] words ''όνος'' (ónos=donkey), ''πέρδω'' (pérdo=to fart), and ''άκανθος'' (ácanthos=thorn), meaning 'donkey fart thorny food'.<ref>[https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/L/Roman/Texts/Pliny_the_Elder/27*.html Bill Thayer, Pliny the Elder: the Natural History, Liber XXVII]</ref><ref>[http://remacle.org/bloodwolf/erudits/plineancien/livre27.htm Pline l'Ancien, Histoire Naturelle, Tome second, Livre XXVII, Traduction française: É. Littré]</ref><ref>[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/27545149 Vaillant S., Etablissement de nouveaux caractères de trois Familles ou Classes de Plantes à Fleurs composées, à savoir des Cynarocéphales..., ''Histoire de l'Academie Royale des Sciences. Avec les Mémoires de Mathematique & de Physique'', Paris 4,: 152, 1718]</ref>

The common name of cotton thistle refers to the [[cotton]]-like hairs on the leaves. Other names are Scots thistle or Scottish thistle, [[Heraldry|heraldic]] thistle and woolly thistle.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN|access-date=18 December 2017}}</ref> The name [[Thistle#Origin as a symbol of Scotland|Scots thistle]] refers to the flower used as the [[Floral emblem#United Kingdom|national emblem]] of [[Scotland]]. However, this is ''[[Cirsium vulgare]]''.{{citation needed|date=May 2019}}, not onopordum.

==Uses==
It is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] for its bold foliage and large flowers.<ref>Holliday, C. (2005). ''Sharp Gardening''. Timber Press {{ISBN|0-88192-699-X}}</ref> It has been used to treat cancers and ulcers and to diminish discharges of mucous membranes. A recent study of a crude extract from the leaves of the plant demonstrated activity against [[glioblastoma]], a type of very malignant brain tumor.<ref>Abusamra YA et.al., 2015. Evaluation of putative cytotoxic activity of crude extracts from Onopordum acanthium leaves and Spartium junceum flowers against the U-373 glioblastoma cell line. Pak J Pharm Sci. 2015 Jul;28(4):1225-32.</ref> The [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]] was eaten in earlier times like an artichoke. The cottony hairs on the stem have been occasionally collected to stuff pillows. Oil from the seeds has been used for burning and cooking.<ref>[http://www.henriettesherbal.com/eclectic/sturtevant/onopordon.html Henriette's Herbal: ''Onopordum acanthium'']</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=M. Grieve |year=1971 |title=A Modern Herbal: The Medicinal, Culinary, Cosmetic and Economic Properties, Cultivation and Folk-Lore of Herbs, Grasses, Fungi, Shrubs & Trees with Their Modern Scientific Uses |publisher=[[Dover Publications]] |location=New York}}</ref>

Thistles produce abundant nectar for pollinators and provide seeds and floss for birds such as the [[European goldfinch|goldfinch]]. Large-flowered tall thistles in particular provide considerable nectar.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://xerces.org/native-thistle-guide/ |title=Native Thistles: A Conservation Practitioner's Guide |last1=Eckberg |first1=James |last2=Lee-Mäder |first2=Eric |last3=Hopwood |first3=Jennifer |last4=Foltz Jordan |first4=Sarah |last5=Borders |first5=Brianna |date=2017 |website=The Xerces Society |publisher=The Xerces Society |access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref><ref name=Pollinators>{{cite web |title=Which flowers are the best source of nectar? |publisher=Conservation Grade |url=http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ |access-date=2017-10-18 |date=2014-10-15 |archive-date=14 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214024659/http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hicks|first1=DM|last2=Ouvrard|first2=P|last3=Baldock|first3=KCR|title=Food for Pollinators: Quantifying the Nectar and Pollen Resources of Urban Flower Meadows|journal=PLOS ONE |volume=11 |issue=6|article-number=e0158117|date=2016|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0158117|pmid=27341588|pmc=4920406|bibcode=2016PLoSO..1158117H|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Pasture Thistle|url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/prairie/plantx/ps_thistlex.htm|website=Illinois Wildflowers|publisher=Dr. John Hilty|access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Bull Thistle|url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/bull_thistle.htm|website=Illinois Wildflowers|publisher=Dr. John Hilty|access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Cotton Thistle, Galong, New South Wales.jpg|thumb|upright|A mature Scotch thistle (1.8 m) at [[Galong, New South Wales|Galong]], Australia]]
[[File:Onopordum acanthium-7-08-04.jpg|thumb|An example of ''Onopordum acanthium'' in southwest Idaho, demonstrating the plant's size]]
In the late 19th century, it was introduced to temperate regions of [[North America]], [[South America]], and [[Australia]] as an ornamental plant, and is now considered a major [[agricultural]] and wildland noxious [[weed]]. It has been recorded from nearly 50 countries.<ref>{{Cite web|publisher=CAB International, 2004|title=Crop Protection Compendium, 2004 edition|url=http://www.cabi.org/compendia/cpc/|author=CAB International|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070716191745/http://www.cabi.org/compendia/cpc/|archive-date=16 July 2007}}</ref> It is difficult to eradicate because of its drought resistance. It can spread rapidly and eventually dense stands prohibit foraging by [[livestock]]. Infestations of cotton thistle often start in disturbed areas such as roadways, campsites, burned areas, and ditch banks. The weed adapts best to areas along rivers and streams, but can be a serious problem in pastures, grain fields and range areas. A single plant is imposing enough, but an entire colony can ruin a [[pasture]] or destroy a park or campsite, sometimes forming tall, dense, impenetrable stands. This issue is often amplified by the prolific thorns found on this species. Besides creating an impenetrable barrier to humans and animals, the plant nearly eliminates forage use by livestock and some mammal species such as [[Red deer|deer]] and [[Moose|elk]].<ref name=issg>[http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=295&fr=1&sts=tss Global Invasive Species Database: ''Onopordum acanthium'']</ref>

In the United States, known infestations include most of the Pacific Northwest along with Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming, Nebraska, and South Dakota. On western rangeland, infestations directly result in significant economic losses for ranchers. It is also widespread in Australia and New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.weeds.asn.au/tasmanian-weeds/view-by-common-name/cotton-thistle/ |title=Tamar Valley Weed Strategy: Cotton Thistle |access-date=19 April 2016 |archive-date=6 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506175951/http://www.weeds.asn.au/tasmanian-weeds/view-by-common-name/cotton-thistle/ }}</ref> In Australia it commonly hybridises with the related invasive ''[[Onopordum illyricum]]''.<ref name=issg/>

===Control===
;Mechanical
Small infestations may be physically removed or cut a few centimetres below the soil surface ensuring that no leaves remain attached to prevent regrowth. Mowing during early flowering will not kill the plant but will reduce seed production. Repeated treatments may be required because populations typically exhibit a wide range of developmental stages among individual plants. Slashing should be done prior to flowering since seed may mature in the seed head after cutting. Plants should not be mowed following seed set, as this increases chances for seed dispersal.<ref name=issg/><ref name=control>[http://www.dpiw.tas.gov.au/inter.nsf/WebPages/RPIO-4ZV6JQ?open Cotton Thistle (Onopordum acanthium L.) Control Guide]</ref>

;Chemical
Because of their shorter life cycle, cotton thistle plants can be effectively treated with herbicides. All herbicide treatments should be applied at the rosette stage of the plant. Generally, herbicide applications would be in early spring or autumn. One of the primary difficulties in chemical control of cotton thistles is their ability to germinate nearly year round. From autumn to spring a range of plant sizes can be found which may result in variable success from chemical control. Herbicides are very effective on seedlings and young rosettes, but control becomes more variable with increasing plant age. ''Onopordum'' spp. seeds may persist for several years in the soil. Buried seed may persist for up to twenty years, and reinfestation is likely without yearly management. Therefore, several years of re-treatment may be necessary. Picloram, dicamba, 2,4-D, dicamba + 2,4,-D, and metsulfuron are effective for controlling cotton thistle.<ref>Beck, K.G. (1991). Biennial thistle control with herbicides. In: James, L.F., J.O. Evans, M.H. Ralphs, and R.D. Child, eds. ''Noxious Range Weeds''. Westview Press, Boulder, Colorado. pp. 254-259.</ref> Clopyralid is more selective for controlling plants in the family Asteraceae, but will also injure or kill legumes.<ref name=issg/><ref name=control/>

;Biological
There are no biological control agents that have been specifically released for cotton thistle control in the United States. A thistle head weevil ''[[Rhinocyllus conicus]]'' that feeds on ''[[Carduus pycnocephalus]]'' has also been shown to feed on cotton thistle. This insect was the object of imprudent biological control introduction, and it became an invasive species that has threatened endangered native thistles in North America (Strong 1997). Establishment of this thistle head weevil as a biological control agent for cotton thistle has been unsuccessful in the Pacific Northwest. A thistle crown weevil (''[[Trichosirocalus horridus]]'') that feeds on musk, bull, plumeless, Italian, and creeping thistles will also feed on cotton thistle. In Australia, this insect has been shown to kill cotton thistle rosettes. The related ''[[Trichosirocalus briese]]'' is also being tested as a control agent.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=D. T. Briese, T. Thomann & J. Vitou |year=2002 |title=Impact of the rosette crown weevil ''Trichosirocalus briesei'' on the growth and reproduction of ''Onopordum'' thistles |journal=[[Journal of Applied Ecology]] |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=688–698 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2664.2002.00747.x |jstor=827177|doi-access= }}</ref> The [[Australian painted lady]] butterfly has been known to use this invasive species as a host plant, but the larvae do not do enough damage to the plant for this butterfly to be used as biological control agent.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Briese|first=D.T.|title=Natural enemies of carduine thistles in New South Wales|journal=Journal of the Australian Entomological Society|year=1989|volume=28|issue=2|pages=125–126|doi=10.1111/j.1440-6055.1989.tb01209.x|doi-access=}}</ref>

In Australia, a total of seven insects have been released to control cotton thistle.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=D. T. Briese |author2=W. J. Pettit |author3=A. Swirepik |author4=A. Walker |year=2002 |title=A strategy for the biological control of ''Onopordum'' spp. thistles in South-eastern Australia |journal=[[Biocontrol Science and Technology]] |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=121–136 |doi=10.1080/09583150120110707|s2cid=85383089}}</ref><ref>Swirepik, A., Smyth, M., 2002. Biological control of broad-leafed pasture weeds (Paterson's curse, Onopordum and nodding thistles): what have we achieved and where to from here?. In: Spafford J.H., Dodd, J., Moore, J.H. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 13th Australian Weeds Conference, Plant Protection of WA, Perth, pp. 373-376.</ref> Two of the seven released insects are [[weevil]]s, including ''[[Larinus latus]]'' which feeds on the seeds, and ''[[Lixus cardui]]'', which bores in the stems.<ref name=issg/><ref name=control/>

;Integrated management
A combination of methods (IPM) is often more effective than any single method. An [[integrated pest management]] plan deals with prevention as well as control. Eradication of weed species is often not a practical goal, but in many cases reducing infestation to manageable levels is an achievable objective. Seed bank longevity is a major factor in managing cotton thistles. Re-establishing competitive perennial grasses and monitoring infested areas on a yearly basis is critical. Herbicides can successfully be used for reducing thistle populations and giving grasses a competitive advantage, but they cannot be used as a stand-alone solution. These techniques must be linked with good grazing practices in rangeland areas. Otherwise, the thistles will recolonize and rapidly replenish the seed bank to pre-control levels.<ref name=issg/>
